T1: Small‑holder farmers and hobbyist gardeners will adopt a differentiated consumer lawn and garden tractor because they need a versatile, affordable machine that can handle multiple tasks, and Deere’s existing tractor engineering provides the necessary performance and reliability. Who benefits: Small‑holder farmers and hobbyist gardeners gain a single machine that can perform multiple tasks, reducing equipment costs and increasing efficiency.. Why behaviour changes: If a consumer perceives a tractor as a versatile tool that can replace multiple hand‑held tools, they will be willing to purchase it and use it for various gardening and farming tasks.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling the tractor directly to consumers or through dealers at a premium price, leveraging its brand reputation for quality and reliability.. Assumptions: Small‑holder farmers and hobbyist gardeners exist in sufficient numbers to justify production and distribution.; They are aware of and willing to purchase tractors for non‑farm uses.; Deere’s existing tractor engineering can be adapted to meet consumer needs without major redesign.. Predictions: If offered, a consumer segment will purchase the tractor at a price above basic lawn mowers but below full‑size tractors.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with a high density of small‑holder farms or hobbyist gardeners..

T2: Homeowners and small property owners will adopt a differentiated consumer lawn and garden tractor because they seek a convenient, time‑saving solution to replace multiple hand‑held tools and are willing to pay a premium for a brand that offers reliability and status. Who benefits: Homeowners gain a single machine that can perform multiple tasks, saving time and labor costs. They also gain status and convenience.. Why behaviour changes: If a consumer perceives a tractor as a status symbol and a time‑saver that can be used for leisure and social activities, they will be willing to purchase it and use it beyond basic lawn care.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling the tractor directly to consumers or through dealers at a premium price, leveraging its brand reputation for quality and status.. Assumptions: Homeowners and small property owners exist in sufficient numbers to justify production and distribution.; They are aware of and willing to purchase tractors for non‑farm uses.; Deere’s existing tractor engineering can be adapted to meet consumer needs without major redesign.. Predictions: If offered, a consumer segment will purchase the tractor at a price above basic lawn mowers but below full‑size tractors.; Sales will be concentrated in suburban and urban areas with high homeowner density..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Small‑holder Farmers vs Homeowners" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view a product description of a basic lawn and garden tractor (no attachments) and are asked: "Which group would be more likely to purchase this tractor?" (a) Small‑holder farmers and hobbyist gardeners; (b) Homeowners and small property owners. They also rate willingness to pay (1‑10) and perceived utility (1‑10). The test will be run with 200 participants (100 per group) over 10‑12 weeks, using a €2,000 budget.. Sample: 200 participants (100 small‑holder farmers/hobbyists and 100 homeowners/small property owners) recruited via online panels in the United States.. Measure: Primary outcome: group preference (small‑holder vs homeowners). Secondary outcomes: willingness to pay and perceived utility scores.. Predictions: T1: Small‑holder farmers/hobbyists will select the tractor as their preferred option and will report higher willingness to pay and utility than homeowners.; T2: Homeowners will select the tractor as their preferred option and will report higher willingness to pay and utility than small‑holder farmers/hobbyists.. Decision rule: If the difference in the proportion of participants selecting the tractor as their preferred option is at least 15 percentage points in favor of the group predicted by the theory, the theory is considered supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, the theory is considered neutral.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare the adoption preferences of small‑holder farmers/hobbyists versus homeowners for a differentiated consumer lawn and garden tractor. The test will provide the necessary evidence to decide whether to invest in a consumer proposition or expand the dealer network. The test budget of €2,000 and 12‑week timeframe are reasonable for this pilot. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare the adoption preferences of small‑holder farmers/hobbyists versus homeowners for a differentiated consumer lawn and garden tractor. The test will provide the necessary evidence to decide whether to invest in a consumer proposition or expand the dealer network. The test budget of €2,000 and 12‑week timeframe are reasonable for this pilot. Target customer: Small‑holder farmers and hobbyist gardeners who need a versatile, affordable machine to perform multiple tasks.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer lawn and garden tractor leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering, offering a single machine that can handle multiple tasks, reducing equipment costs and increasing efficiency.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 200 participants over 10‑12 weeks, using a €2,000 budget.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources published before mid‑1962; the actual demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning remain unknown. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows homeowners selecting the tractor as their preferred option with a 15‑point advantage, T2 would become the favoured theory.; If the test shows small‑holder farmers/hobbyists selecting the tractor as their preferred option with a 15‑point advantage, T1 would remain favoured.; If the test results are inconclusive (less than 15‑point difference), both theories remain uncertain and further testing would be needed.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Test: Marine vs Professional Recommendation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY consumers and professional boat owners/yacht captains. They are shown a product description for Jotun marine coatings, emphasizing either marine expertise (T1) or professional endorsement (T2). They are then asked: "Would you buy this coating for your boat/yacht?" (Yes/No). The test runs for 12 weeks, with 500 participants per condition (1,000 total).. Sample: 500 DIY consumers and 500 professional boat owners/yacht captains recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent measured as binary: Yes/No to buying the coating.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent when the product description emphasizes marine expertise (Yes rate > 55%).; T2: Higher purchase intent when the product description emphasizes professional endorsement (Yes rate > 55%).. Decision rule: If the Yes rate for marine expertise condition is ≥55% and the Yes rate for professional endorsement condition is <55%, then the evidence supports T1. If the Yes rate for professional endorsement condition is ≥55% and the Yes rate for marine expertise condition is <55%, then the evidence supports T2. If both conditions meet the 55% threshold, the evidence is inconclusive.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically validate whether consumers view Jotun as a trusted marine expert and are willing to pay a premium for marine-specific features. The test will provide the necessary evidence to decide whether to proceed with a consumer launch or explore other strategic options. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically validate whether consumers view Jotun as a trusted marine expert and are willing to pay a premium for marine-specific features. The test will provide the necessary evidence to decide whether to proceed with a consumer launch or explore other strategic options. Target customer: DIY consumers and professional boat owners/yacht captains who purchase marine coatings.. Value proposition: A Jotun marine coating that leverages the company’s brand trust and expertise to capture premium pricing and direct-to-consumer sales.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Launch the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the €18,000 budget and 12‑week timeframe.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources available up to mid‑2024; the actual consumer demand for marine coatings and willingness to pay a premium is unknown.. Would change if: If the test shows a purchase intent rate of at least 55% when emphasizing marine expertise, the evidence would support T1 and justify a consumer launch.; If the test shows a purchase intent rate of at least 55% when emphasizing professional endorsement, the evidence would support T2 and justify a different strategic approach.; If the test results are inconclusive (both conditions meeting the 55% threshold), further investigation would be needed to resolve uncertainty.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
